title: SSH Keys
summary: Make an SSH key pair and learn which half is secret and which half you share.
intro:
SSH is a safe way to use the terminal of ANOTHER computer, like a web server or a Raspberry Pi.
Instead of a password, SSH can use a key pair: two files that belong together.
The private key is your secret. The public key is like a lock you can give to any server.
No real server is used here: the folder fake_server/ only pretends to be a server's disk.
In Terminal Academy your home folder (~) is your sandbox, so ~/.ssh is just .ssh here.
outro: You made a real SSH key pair and 'installed' it on a server! Remember the golden rule: the private key never leaves your computer. For real keys, always use a passphrase.

setup.content:
fake_server/ pretends to be a server's disk.
On a real server, your public key would go into /home/student/.ssh/authorized_keys

steps.instruction: SSH keeps its files in a folder called .ssh in your home folder. Create the folder .ssh and make it private (mode 700).
hints: Two commands: mkdir makes the folder, chmod changes who may use it.
steps.explain: 700 means only you can open this folder. SSH is picky: it refuses to use keys that other people could read. The dot at the start makes the folder hidden, so plain ls does not show it (ls -a does).

steps.instruction: Now make a key pair! Create an ed25519 key in the file .ssh/id_academy, with no passphrase (just for practice) and the comment student@academy.
hints: The tool is ssh-keygen. Options: -t = type of key, -f = file name, -N "" = empty passphrase, -C = comment.
steps.explain: You got TWO files: id_academy is the private key (never share it, not even with friends!) and id_academy.pub is the public key (safe to share). The funny picture is the 'randomart', a drawing of your key. For real keys, use a passphrase: then a stolen key file is useless.

steps.instruction: Look at the files in .ssh in long format, so you can see their permissions.
hints: ls -l shows the long format. Add the folder name at the end.
steps.explain: See -rw------- on the private key? That is mode 600: only you can read it. ssh-keygen did that for you. The .pub file is -rw-r--r--, because everybody may read a public key.

steps.instruction: Show your public key on the screen.
hints: It is the file whose name ends with .pub. cat prints a file.
steps.explain: Your public key is just one line: the key type, a long code, and your comment. This line is what you paste into GitHub or send to the person who runs a server. Never cat the private key for someone else!

steps.instruction: Show the fingerprint of your public key (a short ID for it).
hints: ssh-keygen can do more than make keys: -l means 'list the fingerprint', -f picks the file.
steps.explain: A fingerprint is like a short ID card for a key. The long key is hard to compare by eye, but two fingerprints are easy to compare: same fingerprint, same key.

steps.instruction: Install your key on the (fake) server: add your public key to the file fake_server/home/student/.ssh/authorized_keys
hints: cat prints the key, and >> adds it to the end of a file (it creates the file if it is missing).
steps.explain: On a real server, authorized_keys is the guest list: every public key in it may log in. When you connect, SSH proves you have the matching private key, without ever sending it. In real life, ssh-copy-id user@server does this step for you.
